stories.headline: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse
stories.summary: The Go Blog Better HTTP/1 connection reuse Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil 14 October 2026 Take a look at the following function: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code. Using HTTP/1 ( GODEBUG=http2client=0 ), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine.
stories.why_it_matters: On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds. This marks a notable development for engineering teams working in developers.
key_points: Problem & Context: The Go Blog Better HTTP/1 connection reuse Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil 14 October 2026 Take a look at the following function: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Technical Implementation: That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible? The cost of establishing HTTP connections To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.
Deployment & Impact: Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2.

stories.headline: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
stories.summary: arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge.
stories.why_it_matters: Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. This marks a notable development for engineering teams working in technology research.
key_points: Problem & Context: arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon.

Deployment & Impact: Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them.
